Background and Context

Overview Peter Weir’s Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975) opens with a title card dating its events to St Valentine’s Day, 1900: a party of schoolgirls from Appleyard College picnics at Hanging Rock, near Mount Macedon in Victoria, and several members of the party disappear without trace. The film never explains what happened. Instead, it studies how a rigid, ordered colonial society reacts when something happens that its rules, clocks and explanations cannot contain. Knowing where the story comes from, when it is set and how it was made will help you write about Weir’s choices rather than just the plot.

Joan Lindsay’s Novel The film is adapted from Joan Lindsay’s 1967 novel of the same name. Lindsay deliberately blurred fact and fiction, presenting the disappearance as if it might have happened and declining to say whether it did. That ambiguity became part of the story’s legend: many readers and viewers came to believe the events were real. A final chapter that Lindsay cut from the novel, offering a strange, quasi-supernatural resolution, was published after her death; it plays no part in the film.

Analysis You are studying the film, not the novel. Weir keeps Lindsay’s refusal to resolve the mystery and makes it the centre of the viewing experience: the audience, like the characters, is left wanting an answer that never arrives. When you write about ‘unresolved mysteries’, remember that this is a deliberate construction, not a gap.

t: Peter Weir and the Australian New Wave
b: Peter Weir and the Australian New Wave Picnic at Hanging Rock was one of the defining films of the Australian New Wave, a revival of local filmmaking in the 1970s supported by new government film funding. Directed by Peter Weir from a screenplay by Cliff Green, it was a major critical and commercial success and helped bring Australian cinema to international audiences. Appleyard College was filmed at Martindale Hall in South Australia, while the picnic and search scenes were shot at Hanging Rock itself.

t: Peter Weir and the Australian New Wave - Analysis
b: Analysis The New Wave was partly about Australians telling stories about their own landscape and history. Weir’s film looks back at colonial society with a mixture of beauty and unease: the European culture of the college looks lovely but out of place against the ancient Australian bush. This tension between imported civilisation and the land is at the heart of most essay topics.

Victoria in 1900 In 1900 Victoria was still a British colony; Federation would come on 1 January 1901. Wealthy colonial society modelled itself on Britain: its schools taught deportment, French, poetry and the accomplishments expected of young ladies, and its social life was governed by strict rules about class, dress and behaviour. Girls were laced into corsets, gloved and hatted outdoors, and expected to be decorative, obedient and chaste. Class divisions were sharp. The Fitzhuberts are landed gentry; Albert, their groom, is a working man who grew up in an orphanage; Sara, his sister, is a ward whose fees go unpaid. Mrs Appleyard’s college depends on wealthy parents’ money and on its reputation for respectability.

Analysis The rules of this society explain much of what we see: the gloves Mrs Appleyard allows the girls to remove only ‘once the drag has passed through Woodend’, the horror at Miss McCraw being seen without her skirt, the police assumption that the explanation must be a man. Weir shows how fragile these conventions are once they meet something beyond them.

Hanging Rock Hanging Rock is a volcanic formation in the Macedon Ranges, north-west of Melbourne, and lies on the traditional lands of the Dja Dja Wurrung, Taungurung and Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung peoples. Geologically it is relatively young, a point Miss McCraw makes in the film, but in human terms it is ancient. Its jagged pinnacles, narrow passages and balanced boulders give it the maze-like quality Weir’s camera exploits.

Analysis The colonial characters treat the Rock as a picnic spot and a curiosity to be measured. The film suggests that it existed long before them and will outlast them. The settlers’ lack of any real relationship with the land, including the Indigenous history they overlook, is part of what makes it seem so alien and threatening to them.

t: The Look and Sound of the Film
b: The Look and Sound of the Film Cinematographer Russell Boyd gave the film its dreamy, soft-focus look, with diffused light, slow motion and lingering shots of the landscape. The soundtrack mixes Gheorghe Zamfir’s haunting pan flute, original music by Bruce Smeaton, European classical pieces such as the slow movement of Beethoven’s Fifth Piano Concerto, and an unsettling low rumble associated with the Rock.

Social Values

t: Social Values - Order, Rules and Respectability
b: Order, Rules and Respectability Appleyard College values discipline, punctuality and propriety above all. Mrs Appleyard’s instructions before the picnic about gloves, ‘tomboy foolishness’, snakes and returning ‘at about 8’ show a world that tries to anticipate and control every risk. The film questions whether these rules create real order or only the appearance of it: when the girls vanish, the rules offer no answer, and the institution begins to collapse.

t: Social Values - Class and Social Hierarchy
b: Class and Social Hierarchy Wealth and status decide who belongs. Sara, an orphan whose fees are ‘impossibly overdue’, is excluded from the picnic and treated harshly; Mrs Appleyard insists the college is not a ‘charitable institution’. Michael and Albert’s friendship across the class divide stands out as a rare challenge to these values.

Femininity and Restraint The girls are dressed in white, corseted and gloved, praised for beauty and refinement. The film links this ideal of femininity to repression: the girls who climb the Rock shed their shoes, stockings and gloves, and the community’s reaction to the disappearance focuses obsessively on bodies and sexual danger.
Cultural Values

Rationality and Science The characters trust measurement, investigation and explanation. Miss McCraw studies geometry and geology; Sergeant Bumpher interviews witnesses and organises searches; the doctor examines Irma. The film presents a world that does not yield to these methods, suggesting the limits of a purely rational worldview.

t: Cultural Values - European Culture in the Australian Landscape
b: European Culture in the Australian Landscape The college is a piece of England transplanted to the bush: Botticelli prints, Valentine’s poetry, cultivated flowers, high tea and classical music. Weir sets this imported culture against an ancient landscape it does not understand, revealing the colonists’ sense of being outsiders in the land they occupy.

t: Cultural Values - Romanticism and the Sublime
b: Romanticism and the Sublime Some characters, especially Miranda and Michael, are drawn to nature as something beautiful, spiritual and liberating. This Romantic longing for connection with nature coexists with fear: the Rock is both enchanting and terrifying.

Key Ideas and Vocabulary The film can be strange and confusing, so it helps to know the main ideas before you watch. The most fundamental idea is that the natural world is powerful, overwhelming and mysterious, while the human world tries to measure, quantify and make rules to create a sense of control. Weir’s film explores an event that challenges every illusion of control his characters have. The vocabulary below will help you write about each key idea with precision.

t: Key Ideas and Vocabulary - Nature as a Fundamental Force
b: Nature as a Fundamental Force From the opening image of the Rock, the audience sees nature as monumental and powerful. But it is not only the Rock: Weir provides many vignettes of trees, birds, lizards and insects that present the varied, multifaceted natural world beyond human control. Some characters, like Edith, are afraid of and repelled by the untamed bush; others, like Miranda, are drawn to it, literally walking away from the constraints of the human world. Every other idea in the film relates to nature, so any essay on Picnic at Hanging Rock needs to analyse nature in some way. t: Key Ideas and Vocabulary - The Human Need for Rationality and Control
b: The Human Need for Rationality and Control Because life and nature are so overwhelming, people quantify, measure and control the world around them so that they feel powerful and clever. Throughout the film, characters try to explain the mystery of the disappearance, while others recognise the limits of human knowledge. Marion and Miss McCraw measure, calculate and put numbers on the world. As the party approaches the Rock, there is a short discussion about how old it is, as though knowing its age will help them understand it. t: Key Ideas and Vocabulary - Class and Civilisation
b: Class and Civilisation As part of the effort to measure and control the world, humans have created ‘civilisation’, the opposite of the natural world. Appleyard College is its obvious symbol: a monumental colonial building surrounded by a manicured lawn in the middle of the Australian bush. Even nature is controlled there: plants grow in a greenhouse and exotic flowers are arranged in vases. Costume carries the same idea: girls are strapped into corsets every morning, policemen wear brightly polished buttons, Mrs Appleyard’s hair is a carefully coiffed beehive. The characters are arranged into serving classes and ruling classes. Everyone has rules to follow, and the rules make them feel they have tamed the world. As Weir reveals, they have not. Time Time is a tool of measurement, so it belongs with rationality and control, but it is important enough to deserve its own place. The characters are obsessed with time: the girls disappear on a specified date, there are clocks and watches everywhere, and the characters are disturbed when they stop. In contrast stands the natural world, which operates on a scale that is almost incomprehensible: the Rock is millions of years old. Weir also plays with the audience’s sense of time by slowing some of the action down and presenting it in a dreamlike, timeless way. t: Michael and Albert - An Evolving Relationship
b: An Evolving Relationship Through Michael and Albert’s friendship, Weir suggests that the natural world transcends the rigid class divisions of society. Their shared experiences in nature transform both men, while also leaving them disoriented and stripped of certainty. Theirs is the only relationship that genuinely evolves through the film: as they become immersed in the mystery, their friendship mirrors nature’s ability to transcend the social divisions that once separated them. Beginning Middle End Although Albert belongs to a different class, he is friendly and open towards Michael at the picnic, offering to share a drink. Michael returns the friendliness. Albert comments candidly on the girls’ appearance as they cross the stream. When Michael calls him ‘crude’, Albert replies, ‘I say the crude things. You just think ’em.’ Albert believes the girls must be dead, but agrees to help Michael search. He accepts that Michael wants to stay on the Rock overnight and lies to Michael’s uncle for him. Albert finds Michael the next day, recognises the importance of the torn fabric in his hand, then searches the Rock and finds Irma. In Michael’s final scene he shares his dreams with Albert: he can’t help thinking about the Rock; ‘It comes back at night in dreams.’ Albert responds with his own ‘funny dream’, in which he sees his sister Sara, accompanied by the powerful smell of pansies. Dreams At the end of the film both men have dreams. Michael’s is about the Rock; Albert’s is about his sister Sara, which seems random, because for most of the film we did not know they were related. Now, just after Sara has died, Albert dreams about her. Possible readings: for Weir, dreams are symbolic of the mysterious powers of nature; because dreams are disconnected from the rational mind, they symbolise a natural world beyond our control; people and nature are connected in ways that transcend logical thought, and dreams symbolise these connections.

Albert and Sara Albert and Sara are brother and sister, separated in the orphanage. The film never brings them together: Albert does not know his sister is at the college a few miles away, and Sara does not keep in touch with him. On the night of Sara’s death, Albert dreams that she visits him to say goodbye.

Scene Summaries and Analyses The sequences below follow the order of the film. Use them to locate evidence quickly; the Analysis notes suggest how each sequence connects to the big ideas.

Sequence 1 : The Opening Summary : Hanging Rock emerges from mist while Miranda’s voice-over says ‘What we see and what we seem are but a dream, a dream within a dream.’ A title card gives precise factual details about the disappearance. Appleyard College is then shown framed against a foreground of wild summer grass. Analysis : The order is significant. We see the Rock first, then the facts, then the college. From the outset Weir establishes the three forces of the film: nature as a fundamental force, the human need for factual order, and civilisation. The facts tell us what happened but not why, so the film begins with the mystery already unsolved.

Sequence 2 : St Valentine’s Morning Summary : The girls dress, lace each other’s corsets, and exchange Valentine cards and poems. Miranda and Sara share a tender moment. Flowers are everywhere. Mrs Appleyard addresses the girls about gloves, snakes, ‘tomboy foolishness’ and returning ‘at about 8’. Sara is told she is not to go on the picnic. Analysis : Weir portrays the students as elegant, refined and innocent, but also sheltered, uniform and restrained. The cultivated flowers represent a version of nature that has been domesticated and controlled. Mrs Appleyard’s warnings reveal an institutional fear of disorder, danger and lost time.

Sequence 3 : The Picnic Summary : The drag, driven by Mr Hussey, carries the girls, Miss McCraw and Mademoiselle to the Rock. Miranda opens a gate to let the party through. The picnic is laid out with cake, china and white dresses. Nearby, Colonel and Mrs Fitzhubert picnic with their nephew Michael and their groom Albert. Mr Hussey’s and Miss McCraw’s watches are found stopped at twelve. Much of the party grows drowsy and falls asleep. Analysis : The picnic and the characters’ clothing appear incongruous against the ancient landscape; civilised behaviour seems intrusive or strangely detached from the wilderness. The gate is the first threshold between the familiar world and the unknown. The stopped watches signal that the Rock operates outside measured, human time.

Sequence 4 : The Climb Summary : Miranda, Marion, Irma and Edith get permission to take measurements at the base of the Rock. Michael watches them cross the stream; Albert makes crude remarks. The girls climb higher, the rocks becoming increasingly maze-like. Near the top they fall asleep, then wake. Miranda, Marion and Irma, now without shoes and stockings, walk between two great rocks. Edith screams and runs back down. Miss McCraw is seen climbing alone. Analysis : Successive thresholds (the gate, the stream, the narrowing passages) create the sense that the Rock is drawing the girls towards it. Miranda’s line that ‘everything begins and ends at exactly the right time and place’ suggests acceptance of a different kind of time, while Edith’s ‘when are we going home?’ clings to ordinary chronology. Shedding clothes signals liberation from social convention.

t: Sequence 5 : The Return of the Drag
b: Sequence 5 : The Return of the Drag Summary : The drag arrives back at the college late at night. Mrs Appleyard, who has been waiting, hears from Mr Hussey that ‘no one knows... We were asleep.’ Analysis : The schedule Mrs Appleyard imposed has collapsed. Mr Hussey’s admission that everyone was asleep suggests that the rational, conscious mind was absent at the very moment of the event, an early sign that reason will not provide an answer.

Sequence 6 : The Investigation Summary : Sergeant Bumpher leads the inquiry. Edith is examined by the doctor and asked ‘Was there a man?’ Mrs Bumpher reports that the town believes ‘it couldn’t be local.’ Michael first says he saw three girls, then four. Asked what he was thinking of as the girls crossed the creek, he points to a swan vase. Edith returns to the Rock and remembers a red cloud and Miss McCraw climbing in her drawers; Bumpher fixates on the missing skirt. Search parties, a tracker and dogs comb the Rock. Analysis : Each line of inquiry looks for an explanation that fits society’s assumptions: a male attacker, an outsider, a sexual crime. Memory proves unreliable. Bumpher’s dismissal of the red cloud shows that the authorities seek only the kind of explanation that fits their worldview. The film suggests rational thinking can be more concerned with preserving a sense of control than with discovering the truth.

Sequence 7 : Michael’s Search Summary : Against Albert’s advice, Michael rides to the Rock and searches alone, staying overnight. He becomes disoriented, struggles to climb and falls asleep. Albert finds him dazed and injured, clutching a scrap of lace. Following Michael’s trail, Albert discovers Irma alive. Analysis : Michael succeeds where the official searches failed, perhaps because he is guided by emotion and intuition rather than logic. Yet the Rock also overwhelms him, rewarding curiosity while frustrating the desire for certainty.

Sequence 8 : Irma Recovers Summary : Irma recuperates at the Fitzhuberts’ home, shrouded beneath white gauzy fabric. The doctor tells Bumpher her condition is ‘very strange.’ She cannot remember what happened. The townspeople gather, demanding ‘we’ve got a right to know.’ At the college, Miss Lumley calls the news ‘wonderful’; Mrs Appleyard says it ‘makes it worse.’ Analysis : Irma’s return should solve the mystery but instead deepens it. Her lost memory denies rational explanation even to someone who was there. Mrs Appleyard’s reaction reveals her real priority: one survivor with no story is worse for the college than a clear answer of any kind.

Sequence 9 : ‘Tell Us, Irma!’ Summary : Before leaving for Europe, Irma visits the college in a vivid red dress. In the gymnasium, where Sara has been strapped to the wall to cure her stooping, the girls surround Irma demanding answers. The scene becomes hysterical; Miss Lumley cowers behind the piano and Mademoiselle intervenes, slapping Edith. Analysis : Irma’s red links her to the red cloud and suggests she has been transformed. The scene exposes the breakdown of social conventions: fear of the unknown and desperation for answers turn the ‘refined’ young ladies into a mob. Sara’s literal restraint is a stark image of the college’s oppressive control.

Sequence 10 : The College Unravels Summary : Parents withdraw their daughters. Miss Lumley resigns. Mrs Appleyard drinks alone and tells Sara she must return to the orphanage. Sara is later found dead in the greenhouse by the head gardener. That night Albert dreams of his ‘kid sister’. Mrs Appleyard tells Mademoiselle that Sara’s guardian collected her. Analysis : The greatest damage comes not from the Rock but from within the institution. Mrs Appleyard’s need for control turns into cruelty, and the most vulnerable person pays for it. Her lie about Sara shows her preserving appearances to the end.

Sequence 11 : The Ending Summary : At dinner, Mrs Appleyard, dressed more softly than ever before, reminisces about Bournemouth, where ‘nothing changed – ever,’ and wonders how Miss McCraw could ‘allow herself to be spirited away.’ A final voice-over reports that the searches continued without result and that Mrs Appleyard died ‘while attempting to climb the rock.’ The film closes on slow-motion images of the picnic, with Miranda turning to wave. Analysis : Mrs Appleyard, the film’s champion of order, is finally drawn to the Rock herself. Her dishevelled hair and black mourning clothes contrast with her immaculate appearance at the start. The closing return to the picnic, filmed to resemble old footage, leaves the audience suspended in the moment before the disappearance, and suggests that nature is timeless while society can be disrupted and destroyed.

The Opening and Closing Scenes The film opens with a prologue card: On Saturday 14th February 1900 a party of schoolgirls from Appleyard College picnicked at Hanging Rock near Mt. Macedon in the state of Victoria. During the afternoon several members of the party disappeared without trace... This statement sets up the central mystery, but it also suggests a historical event, even though the story is invented. The credits then play over the Rock emerging as if from the mists of time, establishing it as a monument to the endurance of nature, all in under a minute and a half. The film ends with a deep voice explaining what happens to Mrs Appleyard and her college, and noting that the missing girls were never found. The final images are quasi-historical footage of the picnic, in disjointed camera work that further suggests the historical ‘truth’ of the film. Throughout the film, Weir contrasts human lives with the natural world: humans need to understand, measure and create rules for their lives, but nature is impervious to all of them. The scenes that bookend the film make this contrast clear. The prologue outlining a specific date implies that humans need to measure and quantify experiences so that they can understand them. Placing the events in a real, geographical space creates the sense of a real, human tragedy that is recognisable and understandable. Picnicking It seems the only reason anyone goes to Hanging Rock is to picnic. Michael is there with his aunt and uncle (and Albert, although as a servant he has to eat on his own), and the girls of Appleyard College have their own picnic. Both groups eat in a highly ritualised fashion. Michael and his family gather around a tiny table, sipping tea from cups and saucers and staring into space. The girls offer up a toast to ‘St. Valentine’ as Miranda ritualistically cuts the cake. All of this says a great deal about the conventions and customs of the time. Weir deliberately juxtaposes the elements of human civilisation against the ancient bushland. As you watch, look for human objects that seem out of place in the wilderness: the tablecloth, china cups and saucers, the cake, white dresses, parasols, gloves and hats, the drag and its harnessed horses, Mr Hussey’s watch. After the Meal After they have finished eating, Edith looks at Michael’s family and remarks that they ‘might be the only living creatures in the whole world’. Weir then focuses on a group of ants who seem to be having their own picnic of the St Valentine’s cake. By zooming in on the ants, Weir reminds us that the human picnic is only one small event in a teeming natural world that carries on regardless of it, and that civilisation’s rituals are no defence against nature reclaiming what humans leave behind. Having eaten, the humans show how ‘civilised’ they are through actions only humans perform: Mr Hussey wants to know the time. Irma talks about wearing diamonds in the bath. Marion asks if she can take measurements of the Rock. Miss McCraw reads. Mademoiselle compares a human girl to a piece of art. These actions can be read in several ways: human beings are driven by a desire to make sense of their surroundings; people seek order in an otherwise chaotic world; individuals strive to categorise and define the world around them; the pursuit of knowledge reflects a deep-seated need for control; people feel compelled to shape the unfamiliar into a meaningful pattern. Thresholds A threshold is a border between two places; a doorway, for example, is a threshold between the inside of a house and the outside world. Thresholds matter in Picnic at Hanging Rock because there are two distinct worlds in the film: the civilised, confined and restricted world of Appleyard College, and the wild, transcendent natural world of Hanging Rock. To pass from one world to the other, the girls cross physical thresholds that symbolise their transition from one way of thinking and behaving to another. The Stream When Miranda, Marion, Irma and Edith set out to climb the Rock (which they were warned not to do), they must cross a stream. Albert, watching, makes a crude, sexualised remark about the girls’ appearance. Miranda throws a flower into the stream as she crosses, almost like an offering. Weir then provides a close-up of the stream, revealing its murky, organic naturalness. Possible interpretations: Miranda’s flower offering suggests the girls are not simply crossing water: they are entering a kind of ritual, perhaps even making a pact with the natural world. Albert’s voyeuristic commentary frames the crossing as a moment of exposure, as if crossing the stream strips away the girls’ protection and makes them vulnerable. The murkiness of the stream suggests obscured vision, foreshadowing the incomprehensible nature of what is about to occur. The doubling of thresholds creates a sense of inevitability, as though the Rock is drawing the girls towards it through successive layers of boundary.

The Rocks The final threshold is the rocks themselves. At the top, the girls find not a single rock but an immense series of rocks that have formed into tunnels and passageways. Miranda, Marion and Irma disappear through one such passageway at the end of the scene. Michael’s Quest The film is really three intersecting stories: the missing girls, Mrs Appleyard’s victimisation of Sara, and Michael Fitzhubert’s personal journey. In this part of the film, Weir suggests that answers to the mystery cannot be found through rational inquiry alone, but through a willingness to be open to the mystery and power of nature. The big question is: why is Michael the only one who finds a missing girl?

A Different Mindset Michael followed the girls partly up the Rock on the day they disappeared. When Sergeant Bumpher asks ‘As the girls were jumping the creek, what were you thinking of?’, Michael does not answer in words but points to a swan vase containing a native flower (one of the few times a native cut flower is shown). After Michael points to the swan vase, the scene segues to an image of Miranda and then of a real swan. Michael says, ‘I wake up every night in a cold sweat. Just wondering if they’re still alive.’ Albert believes that if ‘the bloody cop and the bloody... tracker and the bloody dog can’t find ’em, well, no one bloody can.’ But Michael believes ‘they may be out there dying of thirst.’ This evidence supports several readings: Michael is guided by emotion rather than logic; he feels a spiritual or mystical connection to Miranda; he is less constrained by conventional society; he has developed a personal connection to the landscape; his youthful imagination lets him see possibilities others cannot; he is undertaking his own journey of self-discovery.

An Individual Search While most characters have given up on finding the girls, Michael cannot let the mystery go. On the first day he searches with Albert and they find nothing. He leaves a trail of note paper to show where he has searched – a rational method. He decides to spend the night on the Rock, sending Albert home to tell his uncle he is staying the night in Woodend. There is an orange-red, mystical sunset. The next day he searches alone. At the top of the Rock he falls asleep, and we hear the voices of the girls describing the Rock from earlier in the film. Mrs Appleyard’s Story Mrs Appleyard is one of the film’s most important characters. She has created the school’s ethos and rules, so she represents a form of institutional authority that seeks to organise and control the lives of women. Her status and reputation depend on how the girls present themselves to the world. When the girls disappear under mysterious circumstances, and evidence emerges that their corsets and clothing had been removed, her standing as a figure of authority, respectability and decorum is irreparably damaged. She is ultimately a tragic figure: like many tragic characters she cannot bend or adapt, clinging desperately to social status, order and control. This rigidity leads to her downfall. She dies, apparently, ‘while attempting to climb the rock’, the natural force that challenged her belief in human order and exposed the limits of her authority.

t: Mrs Appleyard’s Story - Mrs Appleyard’s Setting
b: Mrs Appleyard’s Setting Weir conveys Mrs Appleyard not only through what she wears and how she behaves, but through the spaces she occupies, chiefly her study and sometimes her bedroom. The clock that constantly and audibly ticks in her study conveys her obsession with order, schedules and discipline. The large portrait of Queen Victoria, surrounded by the English flag, above her desk represents her need to display her reverence for authority and status. The pictures of her husband and ancestors on her study walls symbolise her attachment to history and convention. The picture of a tiger on her study wall illustrates both the power of her authority and hidden emotional depths.

t: Mrs Appleyard’s Story - Mrs Appleyard’s End
b: Mrs Appleyard’s End Because Mrs Appleyard represents institutional authority, the events at the Rock, which challenge human order and certainty, have a profound effect on her. On the night before her death, she dines with Mademoiselle de Poitiers, wearing softer, less severe clothing: the only time we see her dressed this way. At dinner, she reminisces about annual holidays in Bournemouth with her late husband, describing it as ‘a delightful place’. She admits she had come to ‘depend so much on Greta McCraw’ and her ‘masculine intellect’, wondering, ‘How could she allow herself to be spirited away?’ The final image of her shows her in black mourning clothes and a funeral veil, staring directly into the camera, as we are told she died ‘while attempting to climb the rock’. Question to answer: What are the consequences of Mrs Appleyard’s controlling mindset?

Unresolved Mysteries You could write an essay about unresolved mysteries that goes: There’s a rock. It does strange things. End of story. It would not get a good mark. Instead, consider the evidence for each mystery and weigh up possible interpretations.

t: Unresolved Mysteries - 1. Why Does Irma Return but the Others Stay Missing?
b: 1. Why Does Irma Return but the Others Stay Missing? Evidence: When Miranda says at the picnic that she no longer wears her pretty jewelled watch, Irma says that if it were hers, she would wear it ‘always... even in the bath.’ Before the girls disappear, Irma says to the prone Edith, ‘Poor Edith. We’ll go back soon.’ Irma cannot recall what happened to her on the Rock. M iranda, M arion and Miss M cCraw are all linked in their names; Irma is different. When Irma revisits Appleyard College, she wears a vivid red dress. The cloud Edith saw at the Rock was red. Possible interpretations: Irma belongs more to the world of civilisation than to the mysterious world of nature; Irma belongs to both worlds; one girl returning heightens the mystery and uncertainty of what happened to the others, a reminder that some mysteries can never be solved; nature allows no rational explanation of its mysteries, even to those who experienced them; Irma has been transformed by her experiences on the Rock, offering a glimpse of what might have happened to the other girls.

t: Unresolved Mysteries - 2. Why Does the Rock Affect People Differently?
b: 2. Why Does the Rock Affect People Differently? Evidence: On the day of the picnic, many characters at the Rock (including Michael’s uncle and aunt) are overcome by sleepiness. While Miranda, Marion and Irma are drawn to the Rock, Edith finds it ‘nasty’. Michael and Albert remain unaffected by the sleepiness that overtakes others on the day of the picnic. When Edith returns to the Rock with Sergeant Bumpher and Mademoiselle, she seems unaffected by its mysterious power. When Bumpher and the first search party climb the Rock, they stop halfway, overcome by heat and exhaustion. When Michael searches the Rock alone, he becomes disoriented, struggles to climb and eventually falls asleep. After Irma returns, the final search shows the party gathered at the base of the Rock in a relaxed, almost picnic-like atmosphere. Possible interpretations: the more people attempt to investigate and control the mysteries of the Rock, the more it resists them; the Rock’s power is shaped by each person’s willingness, or inability, to embrace the unknown; those who approach the Rock with openness are more receptive to its power; the Rock invites people to abandon the constraints of civilisation and enter a timeless world; the Rock reveals people’s true nature rather than affecting everyone the same way; it rewards curiosity but frustrates the desire for certainty; its power cannot be predicted or explained by human logic.

t: Unresolved Mysteries - 3. What Happened to Sara?
b: 3. What Happened to Sara? Weir creates a trail of deliberately conflicting clues about Sara’s fate. Before Mrs Appleyard sees Sara for the last time, Sara sits on her bed beneath a painting of a woman holding two babies, repeating to herself, ‘This is not a charitable institution.’ Mrs Appleyard tells Mademoiselle that Sara’s guardian has come to collect her, though this appears not to have happened. In their final meeting she instead tells Sara, ‘You will be returned to the orphanage.’ Immediately after this, we see luggage being packed into a carriage, although it later becomes clear this is happening at Michael’s house. After her final meeting with Mrs Appleyard, Sara smiles to herself with an expression of quiet resolution. On the night of Sara’s death, Albert dreams of his sister, who tells him, ‘I’ve come a long way to see ya, and now I must go.’ Possible interpretations: Mrs Appleyard drives Sara to end her own life; Mrs Appleyard murders Sara; Sara’s fate mirrors the disappearances, suggesting the Rock’s influence extends beyond the landscape; the search for certainty about Sara’s death is as futile as the search for the missing girls; Sara’s fate shows that human actions in ‘civilisation’ are just as mysterious as nature; Sara escapes institutional control only through death.

t: Unresolved Mysteries - 4. What Happened to Mrs Appleyard?
b: 4. What Happened to Mrs Appleyard? Evidence: In her final scene, Mrs Appleyard wears mourning clothes, as though grieving the loss of her school, her reputation or even herself. In her final scene, she wears an expression of quiet resolve, echoing Sara’s demeanour before her death. She admits she had come to ‘depend’ on Miss McCraw and cannot understand how her masculine intellect could be ‘spirited away... like a silly schoolgirl.’ Possible interpretations: Mrs Appleyard confronts the mysterious power of the Rock and is overwhelmed by it; she is seeking answers at the Rock; she is unhappy with her status and identity and seeks transformation on the Rock; by climbing the Rock herself, she abandons the ordered world she spent her life defending. Activity: Arrange the four mysteries on a spectrum from mysterious, unsettling and disturbing to makes sense, can be accepted . Which do you find least and most explicable, and why?

Time: Finite and Infinite Humans measure time in years, months, weeks, days, all the way down to microseconds, as though it gives them control. Most characters measure out their lives, but there are notable exceptions: Miranda has an almost mystical belief that everything happens at ‘exactly the right time’. One of Weir’s central points is that the natural world has boundless, apparently infinite time, while humans have only a brief, finite time to live. Time as finite and measurable: ‘What time is it?’; the grandfather clock in Mrs Appleyard’s study; the regular beat of classical music; ‘can’t stand the ticking above my heart’ (Miranda, of her watch); the date and year at the opening of the film; Minnie and Tom rushing to get dressed because time has got away from them; ‘Blowed if me watch hasn’t stopped’; ‘When are we going home?’; ‘I’d wear it always’ (Irma, of Miranda’s watch); ‘We’d better be careful. I promised Mrs Appleyard...’. Time as infinite and endless: ‘Everything begins and ends at exactly the right time and place’; slow-motion filming of Miranda; the thrumming of the Rock; ‘What we see and what we seem are but a dream, a dream within a dream’; the haunting pan flutes; the footage of the picnic at the end of the film, simulating the limited frames of historic film; the Rock is ‘quite young, geologically speaking’; ‘Waiting a million years, just for us’; the girls losing track of time and dancing on top of the Rock; the opening shot of Hanging Rock emerging from

b: A Paragraph Frame Topic: In Picnic at Hanging Rock , the natural world is unknowable. Discuss. Topic sentence: From the beginning of Picnic at Hanging Rock , Peter Weir presents the natural world as a mysterious force that can never be fully understood. Initial examples: In the scene where..., Weir suggests that nature...; Through the use of..., Weir emphasises...; This suggests that the natural world... Link: Weir further underlines the mystery of the untamed world through... Further examples: When..., we see that...; By..., Weir illustrates that... t: Organising Evidence for Essays - Unpacking Topics into Sub-Ideas
b: Unpacking Topics into Sub-Ideas To what extent does Picnic at Hanging Rock suggest that the desire to understand the world is ultimately futile? Brainstorm alternatives for ‘understand the world’ and ‘futile’, then choose a sub-idea: The film suggests that humanity’s search for certainty is ultimately defeated by the enduring mysteries of the natural world. Weir portrays the failure of the police investigation as a symbol of the limits of human explanation. By refusing to explain the disappearance, Weir challenges the audience’s assumption that every mystery has a solution. Although the truth remains elusive, the characters’ attempts to understand the disappearance expose important truths about themselves and their society. While Picnic at Hanging Rock denies both its characters and audience definitive answers, it suggests that the search for meaning remains an essential part of the human experience. The film suggests that human systems of order collapse when confronted by nature. To what extent do you agree? Throughout Picnic at Hanging Rock , Weir presents the natural world as a force that exposes the fragility of human attempts to impose order. The disappearance at Hanging Rock reveals how quickly the certainty and structure of society begin to unravel. The film portrays institutions of society as ineffective when faced with forces they cannot explain. The failure of authority figures throughout the film demonstrates that positions of power offer little protection against
Film Techniques

List of Techniques Film Techniques in Picnic at Hanging Rock Technique Definition / Effect Example in the film Extreme long shot Shows a subject from a great distance, often dwarfed by its surroundings. The girls appear tiny against the towering pinnacles of the Rock, emphasising human insignificance. Low-angle shot Camera looks up at a subject, making it seem powerful or threatening. The Rock is frequently shot from below, so it towers over and dominates the characters. High-angle shot Camera looks down on a subject, making it seem small or vulnerable. Marion looks down on the picnickers ‘like a lot of ants’; Mrs Appleyard is often positioned above others. Framing How elements are arranged within the frame to direct attention or suggest relationships. Characters are enveloped by foliage or enclosed by rock walls, appearing subsumed by nature. Slow motion Footage played slower than real time, creating a dreamlike or significant effect. Miranda at the stream and the final picnic images, suggesting a moment outside ordinary time. Soft focus and diffused light Blurred edges and hazy light that soften the image. The morning at Appleyard and the picnic glow like paintings, idealising the girls and the bush. Dissolve One image fades gradually into another, linking them. Michael’s swan vase gives way to Miranda and then to a real swan, linking the three. Voice-over Narration heard over the images. Miranda’s opening ‘dream within a dream’; the closing report of Mrs Appleyard’s death

Framing the Rock How Weir frames the Rock is one of the most reusable pieces of evidence in the film. The camera presents the Rock as something that acts on the characters. Useful vocabulary: What the Rock does (verbs): towers over, dwarfs, encloses, conceals, swallows, lures, beckons, traps, dominates, overwhelms. What the Rock is (nouns): labyrinth, barrier, gateway, prison, predator, refuge, mystery, force, portal, wilderness. What the Rock is like (adjectives): towering, ancient, mysterious, claustrophobic, menacing, alluring, hypnotic, overwhelming, otherworldly, unknowable. How characters are framed within nature: vulnerable, subsumed, enveloped, immersed, diminished, overshadowed. ‘Through low-angle shots that make the Rock tower over the climbing girls, Weir portrays nature as an ancient, dominating force that dwarfs human ambition.’

Sound and Music The soundtrack is one of Weir’s main tools for creating mystery. Notice how each element connects to an idea: Classical music (such as Beethoven) – the human construct of measurable time and European order imposed on beauty. Pan pipes – the timelessness and haunting allure of nature; liberation from social convention. The string quartet and parlour music – the constraints of etiquette and the preservation of social hierarchy. The thrumming of the Rock – the inexplicable power of the natural world and its ancient rhythms. Shrieking, insistent noise – human horror and discomfort in the face of the unknowable. Ticking clocks – humanity’s desire to measure, schedule and control. Science-fiction-like beeping – nature governed by incomprehensible forces; the transcendence of conventional time. ‘Through the soundtrack, Weir demonstrates that humanity’s obsession with measuring time is ultimately pointless when compared with the timelessness of nature.’ Some of the music has a time signature (like most music you hear), some has a drifting, ethereal time signature (the pan pipes), and some has no time signature at all (the thrumming of the Rock). Music also creates mood. Other connections to consider: people’s desire to create structures and societal conventions; the quest for individual identity outside social mores; temporal order imposed on beauty; liberation from social convention; frustration with unanswered questions. Costume Costume tells us about class, conformity and transformation. The schoolgirls: white dresses, gloves and hats suggest elegance, innocence and respectability, but also fragility and restraint. Those who climb remove hats, gloves, shoes and stockings; Edith keeps hers on. Mrs Appleyard: dark, severe dresses, an ornate, old-fashioned hairstyle and a watch pinned to her chest. Later she wears a brooch with her late husband’s photograph, and at the end her carefully arranged hair becomes dishevelled. Miss McCraw: a dark red dress and a veil to keep flies off her face. Mademoiselle: lace blouses, frills, pearls, lace gloves and softly waving hair – elegant and romantic. Miss Lumley: plaid, simple printed blouses, spectacles and muddy colours – sensible, muted, utilitarian. Irma’s return: a vivid red dress among the white uniforms, linking her to the red cloud and marking her transformation. Uniforms: the police, the doctor and the searchers (including the Indigenous tracker in a red coat) are identified by their roles, showing how society organises people by function and class.

t: Sample 1 - Model Picnic at Hanging Rock Essay
b: Sample 1 - Model Picnic at Hanging Rock Essay Topic: How does Weir depict the natural world as a source of both fascination and fear? Introduction In Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975), Peter Weir constructs the Australian bush as a place that draws people in at the very moment it threatens to consume them. Through his framing of the ancient Rock, his treatment of time and the haunting soundscape of the film, Weir presents a landscape that is at once enchanting and menacing to the members of colonial society who visit it. Ultimately, the film suggests that nature’s allure and its danger come from the same source: it lies beyond the reach of human understanding and control. Body Paragraph 1 From the opening sequence, Weir establishes the Rock as an alluring yet ominous presence that overshadows the civilised world. The film begins not with Appleyard College but with the Rock emerging slowly from mist, accompanied by Miranda’s voice-over: ‘what we see and what we seem are but a dream, a dream within a dream.’ By placing the Rock first, before the factual title card and the image of the college, Weir signals that nature is the primary force in the film, older and more powerful than the society that tries to explain it. As the girls climb, low-angle shots make the pinnacles tower over them, while narrow passages enclose them in a labyrinth of stone. The girls are enthralled, gazing upwards as if hypnotised, yet the same framing diminishes them, rendering them vulnerable within a land

Practice Analytical Text Response Topics Topics on The Lottery and Other Stories take the same three shapes as any Section A topic: construction (how does Jackson portray...?), relationship (how two ideas connect) and idea / message (what the stories suggest). Because this is a collection, the strongest essays draw on several stories, and often place examples from two different stories in the same paragraph. Treat ‘The Lottery’ as your anchor story: it shows almost every key idea and technique in the collection. The four key ideas underneath most topics are social judgement and exclusion , insecurity and dissatisfaction , unexpected events that expose our struggles , and the violence and cruelty beneath a civilised society . 1. How does Jackson portray social judgement and exclusion? 2. Challenges to social expectations are treated as threats in Jackson’s stories. Discuss. 3. Jackson’s stories suggest that ordinary social settings can conceal disturbing cruelty. Discuss. 4. How does Jackson depict the pressure to belong in her short stories? 5. The desire for social acceptance shapes the behaviour of many of Jackson’s characters. Do you agree? 6. Jackson’s stories are tales of exclusion and isolation. Discuss. 7. How does Jackson portray the quiet despair hidden within ordinary lives? 8. In Jackson’s stories, dissatisfaction is often a catalyst for imagining alternative realities. Discuss. 9. Jackson’s stories suggest that the search for fulfilment rarely leads to happiness.
Introduction and Context

Overview The Lottery and Other Stories (1949) is Shirley Jackson’s only collection of short stories published in her lifetime. Its twenty-five stories are mostly set in ordinary places: New York apartments, offices, buses and trains, small towns and suburban streets. Jackson finds something unsettling in each of them. Her characters are lonely, dissatisfied or anxious to fit in, and her communities are polite on the surface but capable of exclusion, prejudice and violence. The collection ends with its most famous story, ‘The Lottery’, in which a friendly village gathers on a sunny morning to stone one of its own.

t: America After the Second World War
b: America After the Second World War The stories were written in the 1940s, in the years during and immediately after the Second World War. Post-war America prized stability, prosperity and conformity: suburbs expanded, the ideal family was a breadwinning husband and a homemaking wife, and pressure to fit in was intense. At the same time, the war had revealed how ordinary people could take part in organised cruelty, and the late 1940s saw growing suspicion of anyone considered different or disloyal.

t: America After the Second World War - Analysis
b: Analysis Jackson’s stories expose the anxieties beneath this ideal of order. Her communities enforce sameness, punish difference and turn on outsiders. When you write about conformity, social judgement or ‘the violence beneath a civilised society’, you are writing about fears that were very much alive when Jackson wrote.

Gender Roles Middle-class women in the 1940s were expected to marry, keep house and raise children; single women in the city, like the protagonists of ‘The Daemon Lover’ and ‘The Villager’, lived with the anxiety of ageing outside these expectations. Men were expected to be confident, practical and dominant.

Analysis Many of Jackson’s characters struggle with these roles. Some, like David in ‘Like Mother Used to Make’ or the restless women of ‘The Tooth’ and ‘Elizabeth’, do not fit them; others, like Tessie Hutchinson with her dishes in the sink, play them dutifully until it is too late. Jackson shows both the pressure to conform and the price of conforming.

Race and Prejudice America in the 1940s was deeply segregated, and racism was often expressed through polite, respectable behaviour rather than open hostility. Two stories, ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’ and ‘Flower Garden’, examine this directly.

Analysis Jackson is interested in the gap between how people see themselves and how they behave. Mrs Wilson thinks she is generous; the people of the town think they are protecting their community. Both stories show prejudice maintained by people who believe themselves to be good.

The Reception of ‘The Lottery’ ‘The Lottery’ was first published in The New Yorker in June 1948. It provoked one of the largest reader responses in the magazine’s history: hundreds of letters, many angry, confused or disturbed, and some asking where such lotteries were held. Readers were shocked that a story could show ordinary, likeable people carrying out a murder as calmly as a town meeting.
Analysis The reaction proves Jackson’s point. Readers recognised the village as their own, which is exactly what made the story so disturbing. Its power comes from its ordinariness.

t: Shirley Jackson and the Short Story
b: Shirley Jackson and the Short Story

Shirley Jackson (1916–1965) Shirley Jackson was born in San Francisco and spent most of her adult life in North Bennington, Vermont, where her husband, the critic Stanley Edgar Hyman, taught at Bennington College. She raised four children while writing novels, short stories and humorous accounts of family life. As an outsider in a small New England town, she experienced the kind of suspicion and gossip her stories depict. She is best known today for ‘The Lottery’ and for her novels The Haunting of Hill House (1959) and We Have Always Lived in the Castle (1962), and is regarded as a major writer of psychological suspense and the uncanny.

Why the Short Story? A short story has little room for explanation. Jackson uses this to her advantage. She often: opens with a description of the protagonist’s ordinary routine or a pleasant setting; introduces an unexpected event, stranger or disruption; lets tension build through small, everyday details and dialogue; ends abruptly, often with the protagonist excluded, defeated or trapped, and without explaining what it all means. The reader is left to fill the silence, and that is where much of the unease comes from.

t: Reading the Collection as a Whole
b: Reading the Collection as a Whole Although each story stands alone, the collection is designed to be read together. A figure named James Harris (or Jim, or Jamie) appears in many stories in different guises: a missing fiancé, a writer, a dinner guest, a neighbour, a stranger in a blue suit. The book is divided into parts introduced by epigraphs from Joseph Glanvill’s seventeenth-century treatise on witchcraft, and ends with an epilogue: verses from the old ballad ‘James Harris, The Daemon Lover’, in which a mysterious lover carries a woman away to her doom.

t: Reading the Collection as a Whole - Analysis
b: Analysis These links suggest that the strangeness in each story is part of a larger pattern. James Harris works almost like a demon or tempter who drifts through ordinary lives, exposing the dissatisfaction and fear already present beneath the surface. In essays, connecting stories through these recurring figures and motifs shows the examiners that you understand the collection, not just individual stories.

t: Structure and Themes in The Lottery and Other Stories
b: Structure and Themes in The Lottery and Other Stories

t: How the Stories Can Be Grouped
b: How the Stories Can Be Grouped This guide concentrates on twelve stories that together cover the collection’s key ideas. A useful way to study them is in groups: Discontent and identity: ‘The Daemon Lover’, ‘Like Mother Used to Make’, ‘The Villager’ Cruelty taught and normalised: ‘The Witch’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘Charles’ Insiders and outsiders: ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’, ‘Flower Garden’ Challenging or yielding to expectations: ‘Elizabeth’, ‘The Tooth’, ‘Of Course’ The anchor story: ‘The Lottery’

Unexpected Events Expose Our Struggles Jackson uses unexpected events and strangers to expose characters’ hidden fears, insecurities and dissatisfaction with their lives. A fiancé fails to arrive; a stranger knocks on the door; a man on a train tells a child a violent story. The disruption does not create the problem so much as reveal what was already there.

Insecurity and Dissatisfaction Jackson shows how people feel uncertain about their identities and dissatisfied with their lives, often imagining that another life might make them happier. The protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ is ‘not satisfied with her clothes, her face, her apartment’; Miss Clarence in ‘The Villager’ once wanted to be a dancer; Clara Spencer in ‘The Tooth’ drifts away from her own identity altogether.

Social Judgement and Exclusion Jackson explores how social expectations pressure people to conform and leave those who do not fit in feeling judged, anxious and excluded. Mrs MacLane is frozen out of the town in ‘Flower Garden’; Mrs Walpole fears her neighbours in ‘The Renegade’; Tessie Hutchinson is cast out in the most final way possible.

t: The Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society
b: The Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society Jackson reveals how violence, cruelty and hostility can exist beneath the polite and orderly surface of everyday life. Physical violence features in only a few stories, so think of this idea more broadly: cruelty, insensitivity, aggressive intolerance and a lack of compassion. Strangers mock, neighbours gossip, children learn to relish violence, and a whole village picks up stones.

Endings Jackson’s stories often end grimly, and these endings are some of the most useful evidence you have. Compare: ‘The Daemon Lover’: ‘No matter how often or how firmly she knocked, no one ever came to the door.’ ‘Like Mother Used to Make’: David thinks miserably of his own warm home and hears faintly down the hall the sound of laughter. ‘The Villager’: ‘Her shoulders ached.’ ‘The Witch’: ‘Prob’ly he was a witch.’ ‘The Renegade’: Mrs Walpole closes her eyes, ‘suddenly feeling the harsh hands pulling her down, the sharp points closing in on her throat.’ ‘Flower Garden’: Mrs Winning ‘swung around without speaking and started, with great dignity, back up the hill toward the old Winning house.’ ‘The Lottery’: ‘It isn’t fair, it isn’t right,’ Mrs. Hutchinson screamed, and then they were upon her. Some endings shut characters out (exclusion); some leave them trapped in disappointment (defeat and resignation); some show cruelty becoming normal. Very few offer justice or resolution.
Language and Style

An Understated, Ordinary Voice Jackson writes in a plain, calm, almost conversational style. She describes terrible things in the same tone as a morning’s errands. In ‘The Lottery’, the stoning is introduced through the same matter-of-fact narration as the gathering of the villagers and their chat about tractors and taxes. This flatness is deliberate: by refusing to signal horror, Jackson makes the reader feel the horror of how normal cruelty has become.

Everyday Detail Jackson builds her worlds from small, concrete details: coffee, dishes in the sink, the neat chairs in David’s apartment, a lollipop, a bus ticket. These details make the settings feel real and familiar, which is what makes the disruptions so unsettling. They also carry meaning: the protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ repeatedly finds ‘nothing to eat’, and her lack of appetite suggests the emptiness of her life.

Dialogue and Polite Speech Characters in Jackson’s stories are often unfailingly polite while saying cruel or prejudiced things. Mrs Wilson’s generosity in ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’ is full of assumptions; the neighbours in ‘The Renegade’ cheerfully suggest ways to kill a dog; Mrs Harris in ‘Of Course’ imposes her views through seemingly friendly conversation. Listen for the gap between the tone of what is said and what it means.

Irony Irony runs through the collection: a lottery whose ‘prize’ is death; a sunny summer day for a murder; a title, ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’, that mocks performative politeness; a mother in ‘Charles’ who never suspects the badly behaved boy is her own son.

Unnamed and Symbolic Names Some characters have no name at all: the protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’, ‘the little boy’ in ‘The Witch’. This makes them seem anonymous and interchangeable, as if their stories could belong to anyone. Other names are pointed: Laurie suggests a crown of laurels, a symbol of glory; Walpole has been read as meaning ‘foreigner’; Clara means ‘clear’ or ‘bright’; Mrs Winning belongs to the family that always wins.

Setting and Weather Jackson often sets disturbing events against pleasant weather. The village of ‘The Lottery’ gathers on a ‘clear and sunny’ morning ‘with the fresh warmth of a full-summer day’. Ask whether the weather in a story reinforces ordinary life, contrasts with it, mirrors the characters’ feelings, or creates an ironic contrast with them.

Open Endings Jackson rarely explains. We never learn what happened to Jamie Harris, who the man on the train really was, or where Clara Spencer is going. The reader is left uneasy, and must decide for themselves what the story reveals.
Story Summaries and Analyses The collection contains twenty-five stories. The twelve below are the key stories for essays: learn them well enough to use them flexibly across many topics.

‘The Daemon Lover’ Summary : On the morning she is to marry Jamie Harris, an unnamed woman of thirty-four prepares anxiously, changing her dress, tidying her apartment and stocking food for their new life. Jamie does not arrive. She goes looking for him, questioning shopkeepers, a newspaper seller and neighbours, who respond with indifference, suspicion or mockery. Following vague leads, she reaches an apartment building where she thinks she hears voices and laughter behind a door, but no one answers her knocking. Analysis : The protagonist is defined by deep-seated dissatisfaction: she is ‘not satisfied with her clothes, her face, her apartment’ and hopes marriage will transform her life. The recurring lack of food (‘There was nothing to eat in the apartment’) suggests a life that is empty and hollow. ‘Daemon’ can mean demon, but also a guiding or inspiring spirit; Jamie is both, offering hope and then vanishing cruelly. The casual cruelty of strangers (‘the boy grinned insolently at her’) shows how easily individual suffering is dismissed. The ending, with the door that never opens, is one of Jackson’s starkest images of exclusion.

‘Like Mother Used to Make’ Summary : David Turner keeps a neat, carefully chosen apartment and enjoys cooking and domestic order. His neighbour Marcia is loud, untidy and always hungry. David invites her to dinner and bakes a cherry pie. When Mr Harris, a man from Marcia’s office, knocks, Marcia lets him assume the apartment and the cooking are hers. David, unable to assert himself, is gradually pushed out and ends up retreating to Marcia’s cluttered apartment, hearing laughter from his own home down the hall. Analysis : Jackson contrasts David’s control (‘small, quick movements’, ‘the neat small table and four careful chairs’) with Marcia’s disorder (‘Marcia arrived with a shout and fresh air and disorder’). David’s pleasure in domestic activities challenges traditional ideas of masculinity, and his passivity leaves him excluded from his own home. The title is ironic: the comforts of home ‘like mother used to make’ are made by a man and claimed by a woman who did not make them.

‘The Villager’ Summary : Miss Hilda Clarence, a woman in her thirties who came to New York hoping to be a dancer, now works in an office. She visits an apartment to look at furniture for sale. While waiting, she is mistaken for the owner by a visitor named Harris, and slips into the role, inventing a life as a ‘dancer’. After he leaves, she returns to her own reality. Analysis : Harris’s unexpected arrival is the catalyst that exposes Miss Clarence’s disappointment with her life. She tells herself she has ‘a good job’ and lives ‘better than she would have in her home town’, but her compulsive lie reveals her desire to be seen as someone more accomplished and interesting. The final line, ‘Her shoulders ached’, suggests the weight of carrying unfulfilled dreams.

‘The Witch’ Summary : A little boy travels by train with his mother and baby sister, looking out the window. A friendly stranger sits beside him and, encouraged by the boy’s questions, tells a gruesome story about killing his own little sister. The mother is horrified, but the boy is delighted. When the man leaves, the mother tries to explain it away, and the boy decides ‘Prob’ly he was a witch.’ Analysis : The story shows how children learn what behaviour is normal. The baby ‘strapped securely to the seat’ and the boy rewarded with a lollipop suggest a world of control and reward, yet the boy greets violence with breathless excitement (‘Did you cut her all in pieces?’). The cruelty arrives in a pleasant, everyday setting, which makes it more disturbing. The boy’s final explanation turns real violence into a fairy tale.

‘The Renegade’ Summary : Mrs Walpole, new to the country, learns that her family’s dog, Lady, has been killing a neighbour’s chickens. As she goes about the town, neighbours offer increasingly cruel advice for curing or punishing the dog, including tying a dead chicken around her neck or fitting her with a spiked collar. When her own children eagerly describe how the spikes would cut the dog’s head off, Mrs Walpole feels as though she is being attacked herself. Analysis : A renegade is someone who rejects conventional behaviour; the dog is one, but so in a sense is Mrs Walpole, an outsider in the community. The neighbours’ casual enthusiasm normalises violence, and her children’s delight shows how readily cruelty is passed on. The ending, ‘the harsh hands pulling her down, the sharp points closing in on her throat’, transfers the punishment from the dog to the woman, revealing her fear of the community’s judgement.

‘Charles’ Summary : Laurie starts kindergarten and comes home each day with stories about a boy called Charles who misbehaves dreadfully. His parents are fascinated and amused, and ‘Charles’ becomes a family byword. At the parent-teacher meeting, Laurie’s mother looks for Charles’s mother, only to learn from the teacher that there is no Charles in the class. Analysis : Laurie invents an identity to conceal his own bad behaviour, and his mother’s unquestioning acceptance shows how parents see what they want to see. The twist exposes the gap between appearance and reality, and the comic tone hides a sharper point about how adults misread, and help create, children’s behaviour.

‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’ Summary : Johnny brings his friend Boyd, a Black boy, home for lunch. Johnny’s mother, Mrs Wilson, assumes Boyd’s family is poor, his father a labourer, and his mother overworked, and offers him charity he does not need. Boyd politely corrects each assumption. Mrs Wilson becomes offended when he declines her old clothes, while the boys, untroubled, carry on with their game. Analysis : The title comes from a comic strip about two absurdly polite Frenchmen who keep deferring to each other; the boys use it to play at manners. Jackson uses it ironically to expose the gap between outward politeness and genuine respect. Mrs Wilson believes she is being kind, but her ‘kindness’ is built on racist stereotypes, and her defensiveness shows how entrenched they are.

‘Flower Garden’ Summary : Young Mrs Winning, who has married into the town’s oldest family and lives under her mother-in-law’s control in the old Winning house, befriends Mrs MacLane, a widow who moves into the cottage she herself once dreamed of owning. The two women grow close, and their sons play together. When Mrs MacLane hires a Black man, Mr Jones, to help with her garden, the town turns against her, and Mrs Winning, fearing association, abandons her. Analysis : The townspeople act as gatekeepers, advising Mrs Winning to speak to Mrs MacLane ‘about that colored man’. Mrs MacLane recognises what is happening: ‘Pretty soon they... they’ll tell someone else to speak to me.’ Children reveal the town’s values: Howard’s racist name-calling towards Billy Jones shows how early prejudice is learned. The ending, as Mrs Winning walks ‘with great dignity’ back to the old house, shows conformity winning over friendship.

‘Elizabeth’ Summary : Elizabeth Style works for a struggling literary agency in New York, in a relationship with her business partner that has lost its warmth, and in a life far from the success she once imagined. When a new secretary arrives, Elizabeth feels her position slipping. The story ends with her making a dinner date with Jim Harris, who she hopes might help launch a new career. Analysis : Elizabeth’s story is one of insecurity and quiet despair beneath a professional surface. Her plans with Harris represent the possibility of another life, but the reader suspects they are another illusion. Like the protagonists of ‘The Daemon Lover’ and ‘The Villager’, she pins her hopes on a man who may never deliver.

‘The Tooth’ Summary : Clara Spencer takes an overnight bus to New York to see a dentist about a painful tooth. Dazed by codeine and lack of sleep, she meets a man in a blue suit, Jim, who speaks of a beautiful faraway place. In the city, her sense of self dissolves; she cannot remember details of her own life and must find her name written on her belongings. At the end she runs barefoot through hot sand, hand in hand with Jim. Analysis : Jim represents Clara’s desire to escape her ordinary, grey life. His poetic visions (‘the waves ringing on the shore like bells’, ‘the grass is so green and so soft’) evoke a mythical place far from bus stations and dentists’ rooms. Clara’s name means ‘clear’ or ‘bright’, ironic for a woman whose identity has faded. Unusually, the ending suggests escape from social expectations rather than defeat, though whether it is liberation or madness is left open.

‘Of Course’ Summary : Mrs Tylor watches new neighbours move in next door and decides from their furniture and clothes that they are ‘nice people, obviously’. When she speaks to Mrs Harris, however, she learns that the family does not allow movies, radio or newspapers. Mrs Tylor, unsettled, finds herself agreeing politely. Analysis : The story turns on the pressure of neighbourliness. Mrs Tylor’s first judgements are based on appearances; Mrs Harris then projects her own rigid views through friendly conversation (‘it means such a lot to have really thoughtful neighbors’). Social conformity and the appearance of politeness are maintained, despite the intolerance beneath them.

‘The Lottery’ Summary : On the morning of June 27th, the villagers of a small farming community gather in the square for their annual lottery. Children collect stones. Mr Summers runs the drawing from a battered black box. Tessie Hutchinson arrives late, joking that she forgot what day it was. Heads of families draw slips of paper; Bill Hutchinson draws the marked slip. Tessie protests that it ‘wasn’t fair’, and in a second drawing among the Hutchinson family she draws the paper with the black spot. The villagers, including her friends and children, stone her. Analysis : ‘The Lottery’ is the anchor story of the collection: it shows every key idea. The pleasant setting (‘clear and sunny’) makes the violence more shocking. The ritual is maintained by authority figures (Mr Summers, Mr Graves), defended by Old Man Warner (‘There’s always been a lottery’), and carried out by ordinary people. Mr Adams mentions villages that have given up the lottery, yet still joins in. Tessie is no rebel: she accepts the lottery until it threatens her. The detail that ‘although the villagers had forgotten the ritual and lost the original black box, they still remembered to use stones’ suggests that the violence outlives any meaning the tradition once had.

‘The Witch’ A young boy takes a train ride with his mother and baby sister. The mother keeps the baby quiet by constantly feeding her toast and largely ignores her son’s questions and comments, casually teaching her children compliance. When a strange man sits down and tells the boy a shockingly violent story, the boy is delighted and the mother horrified. When the man suggests chopping off his little sister’s head, the boy concludes that the man is a ‘witch’, someone who lives beyond the conventions of normal society. Annotate: Violence lies beneath the veneer of civilised behaviour – excitement about violence. Social pressure and parenting create conformity – windows to an outside, different world; food and lollipops; the straps that hold the baby in a sitting position. ‘The Lottery’ A lottery is a form of gambling in which names or tickets are placed in a box and one is drawn at random, usually to win a prize. Because lotteries are so familiar, Jackson presents the ritual as calm, ordinary and completely accepted. The villagers gather, chat and wait as though taking part in a harmless community tradition, and this unsettling normality gives the story its disturbing atmosphere. Gradually the reader discovers that the ‘winner’ receives no reward but is violently sacrificed by the community. Through this shocking ending, Jackson shows how societies can destroy individuality and morality through blind conformity to tradition. Connecting the Stories When you study a collection, you need to make connections between stories that can seem completely different. The activities below practise linking stories through shared ideas, symbols and character types, which is exactly what high-scoring Section A essays do.

Naming, or Not Naming, Protagonists Many of Jackson’s protagonists have no name. The protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ is never named, although her fiancé and many people she meets are. By contrast, David Turner’s name opens ‘Like Mother Used to Make’. Describing the two protagonists. The protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ is nebulous, unsure, uncertain, undecided, operating in a liminal space, between life stages, doubtful, searching for direction, plagued by self-doubt, torn between possibilities (of/about herself, who she is, her identity, who she would like to be). David Turner is definite, particular, sure, individual, well defined, set in his habits, secure, clear about, guided by firm principles, anchored by routine (about himself, who he is, his identity, his aspirations). In ‘The Daemon Lover’, the unnamed protagonist wanders through the city searching for her missing fiancé. As she moves through apartments, streets and memories, she struggles to define herself outside the expectations of romance and marriage. Windows and Doors In Jackson’s stories windows are highly symbolic: when characters look out of them, they are often thinking about a different life they could have lived. ‘The Daemon Lover’: ‘She went to the window and saw that it was undeniably a fine day. It occurred to her that perhaps she ought not to wear the blue silk dress; it was too plain, almost severe, and she wanted to be soft, feminine.’ ‘Like Mother Used to Make’: ‘The window had been open all day and papers had blown wildly around the floor. David closed the window, hesitated over the papers, and then moved away quickly.’ ‘The Villager’: ‘The first thing Miss Clarence did was go to the window... far off to the left, a high building crowned with flower gardens. Someday I’ll live there, she thought.’ ‘The Witch’: ‘The little boy was looking out the window... “I saw a witch,” he said.’ In each, a character is having one kind of experience in their own world while seeing, or avoiding, a different kind of experience through the window. Social Judgement Across the Stories One of the powerful forces oppressing Jackson’s characters is the social judgement they all feel. Her protagonists spend a lot of energy worrying about what others will think. ‘The Daemon Lover’: ‘Why don’t I go to the police–you go to the police for a missing person. And then thought, What a fool I’d look like.’ She is worried about looking foolish and being pitied. ‘The Villager’: ‘He wandered over and opened the bathroom door; when he glanced in Miss Clarence winced.’ She is worried that the dirty bathroom will be judged as hers. ‘The Renegade’: ‘anyone would tell on a chicken-killing dog; but he doesn’t have to be so pleased about it.’ Mrs Walpole is worried that her neighbours are enjoying her humiliation. The protagonists also judge others and themselves: the protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ judges her own appearance and apartment; David judges the clerks who don’t recognise him; Miss Clarence judges the Robertses’ housekeeping; Mrs Walpole judges her own failures against the ‘country folk’. In comparison, many minor characters seem almost immune to judgement: the stranger in ‘The Witch’ doesn’t care what the mother thinks; the Robertses leave their messy apartment open for others to see; the grocer and the other men in ‘The Renegade’ don’t consider how the dog’s owner feels. Racism and Social Judgement The racism in ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’ and ‘Flower Garden’ is part of Jackson’s larger concern with how social judgement shapes society. Racism controls not only its victims, like Mr Jones in ‘Flower Garden’, but also those who act with prejudice. Like any form of social judgement, it makes everyone unhappy. Theme Analysis

Insecurity and Dissatisfaction Jackson’s protagonists are frequently discontented. The woman in ‘The Daemon Lover’ suffers from deep-seated dissatisfaction, anxiety about her appearance and ageing, and insecurity about her desirability; she hopes marriage will let her reinvent herself. Miss Clarence in ‘The Villager’ disguises her disappointment that she never became a dancer. Elizabeth Style pins her hopes on Jim Harris. Clara Spencer escapes her grey life entirely, at the cost of her identity. Jackson suggests that these characters’ unhappiness is shaped both by society and by themselves. Social expectations about marriage, success and femininity set the standards they fail to meet, but their own fantasies of another life deepen their dissatisfaction. As one useful interpretation puts it, the protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ intensifies her own unhappiness through her thoughts, choices and actions, while the happiness of others accentuates her dissatisfaction.

Social Judgement and Exclusion Jackson’s communities decide who belongs. People who challenge social expectations are judged, excluded or punished: Mrs MacLane for employing Mr Jones, Mrs Walpole for her uncontrolled dog, David for failing to be the right kind of man. Insiders police the boundaries out of fear of becoming outsiders themselves: Mrs Winning abandons her friend because she is anxious about losing belonging and respectability. Useful vocabulary: conformity, gatekeepers, ostracise, marginalise, alienated, exclusionary, respectability, social status .

Unexpected Events Expose Our Struggles A stranger arrives, a fiancé disappears, a dog kills chickens, a man on a train tells a story. In each case, the disruption exposes problems that already existed beneath the surface: Miss Clarence’s disappointment, David’s passivity, Mrs Walpole’s fear of her neighbours, the mother’s inability to control what her son learns. James Harris, who appears in story after story, embodies this idea: he enters characters’ lives unexpectedly and reveals the gap between how they see themselves and how others see them. Useful vocabulary: catalyst, disruption, destabilise, unravel, expose, vulnerability .

t: The Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society
b: The Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society Physical violence features in only a few stories (‘The Witch’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘The Lottery’), so think of this idea as including cruelty, insensitivity, intolerance and lack of compassion. Jackson’s violence is often: Arbitrary – based on chance rather than any fair reason, like the lottery’s random selection; Ritualised – performed according to tradition, like the annual drawing; Normalised – treated as ordinary even when it is harmful, like the neighbours’ advice in ‘The Renegade’; Entrenched – so established that it is difficult to change, like the racism of ‘Flower Garden’. Jackson repeatedly shows that the most disturbing cruelty comes from ordinary, respectable people: friendly neighbours, polite mothers, children. Children both reveal the hidden prejudices of adults and occasionally resist them, highlighting the flaws in adult values.

Conformity and Tradition Many stories show a chain of social pressure: society establishes rules about how people should behave; adults teach children what is normal; fear of punishment pressures people to conform; people come to accept the rules without questioning them; and harmful attitudes are passed from one generation to the next. In ‘The Lottery’, even little Davy Hutchinson is given pebbles.

t: Key Vocabulary for the Four Ideas - Social Judgement and Exclusion

Most of Jackson’s protagonists break with what is ‘accepted’ in some way, and feel uneasy about not fitting in and anxious about their choices. Many feel strongly that they should go along with the unwritten rules of dominant values. t: Key Vocabulary for the Four Ideas - Insecurity and Dissatisfaction
b: Insecurity and Dissatisfaction Many protagonists feel insecure about their life choices or identity. Even characters who seem certain daydream about alternative lives or feel unhappy about some aspect of their lives. They often express insecurity by imagining different lifestyles, and they regularly look out of windows or through doorways while doing so. Another sign of self-doubt is choosing clothes and feeling that none of their outfits, belongings or homes are right.
